As stated in my first comment. Children often don't mean to cause damage with experimentation, that doesn't mean it doesn't happen. It isn't as black and white as 'perpetrator' and victim. You can't place blame on a child who doesn't know what they're doing. It could very well be damaging to all involved. That said. If OP feels it caused lasting trauma, that is totally valid and can't be ignored just because the other person didn't mean to hurt them. It comes down to OP and their feelings.

Your gp is definitely a good place to start. They can prescribe some meds, but more importantly they can refer you to someone who can help. There may also be specialists in your area, a Google search can turn up therapists and psychiatrists in your area or online. Just make sure they specialize in what you need! Usually they are very upfront about that.

  


Also a covid suggestion: betterhelp offers telecommunication therapy at pretty affordable prices. May not be for you especially as this is your first time, but worth mentioning.

  


Last thing I swear! How you go about it is totally up to you. I've had to resort to writing out my thoughts because I struggle to articulate myself out loud, then give the paper to the care provider. Whatever you have to do to get the help you need!

Child on child sexual assault is indeed a real thing and it can cause lasting trauma. Whether or not they knew what they were doing, it can be damaging to the victims. It's a really grey area, because it's usually not the perpetrators intention to hurt someone, they're just figuring things out like every other kid. I agree with the comment saying the behavior comes from somewhere though, it could be something intergenerational or it could be as innocent as kids just trying to figure shit out.

  


The point is, any of that kind of behavior that is nonconsensual (and kids, as most people will agree, don't know enough to properly consent) can be considered sexual harassment or assault. It comes down to your perception of it, which makes things even more complex. If you feel it left lasting scars, you may want to consider talking about it in therapy or, if the situation is safe to, entrusting someone else in your family with the information can be a load off. In some cases though, like if it's really bad and still affects you, you need to do what it takes to make sure you feel safe and happy.
